claim: Influenza virus has a high mutation rate, such that within one host different viral variants can emerge.
source: Influenza virus has a high mutation rate, such that within one host different viral variants can emerge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about influenza virus biology in the abstract.

claim: Influenza virus variants are more prevalent in pregnant and/or obese individuals due to their impaired interferon response.
source: Evidence suggests that influenza virus variants are more prevalent in pregnant and/or obese individuals due to their impaired interferon response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research as indicated by the phrase 'Evidence suggests'.

claim: The non-allergic, paucigranulocytic subtype of asthma is associated with impaired type I interferon production.
source: We have recently shown that the non-allergic, paucigranulocytic subtype of asthma is associated with impaired type I interferon production.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous research.

claim: Mice with paucigranulocytic asthma had increased disease severity compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, mice with paucigranulocytic asthma had increased disease severity and an increased emergence of influenza virus variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Mice with paucigranulocytic asthma had an increased emergence of influenza virus variants compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, mice with paucigranulocytic asthma had increased disease severity and an increased emergence of influenza virus variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by sequencing data in the manuscript.

claim: PB1 mutations exclusively detected in asthmatic mice were associated with increased polymerase activity.
source: Specifically, PB1 mutations exclusively detected in asthmatic mice were associated with increased polymerase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by minigenome assay data.

claim: Asthmatic host-derived virus led to increased disease severity in wild-type mice.
source: Furthermore, asthmatic host-derived virus led to increased disease severity in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in wild-type mice.

claim: At least a subset of patients with asthma may be more susceptible to severe influenza.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that at least a subset of patients with asthma may be more susceptible to severe influenza and may be a possible source of new influenza virus variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Patients with asthma may be a possible source of new influenza virus variants.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that at least a subset of patients with asthma may be more susceptible to severe influenza and may be a possible source of new influenza virus variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about viral variant emergence.

claim: The influenza virus RNA polymerase has poor proofreading activity, resulting in a high rate of viral mutations.
source: Similar to many other RNA viruses, the influenza virus RNA polymerase has poor proofreading activity, resulting in a high rate of viral mutations (Van den Hoecke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Even if an influenza virus infection occurs with a defined molecular clone, there will be rapid generation of viral variants that possess one or more mutations relative to the original virus strain.
source: Accordingly, even if an influenza virus infection occurs with a defined molecular clone, there will be rapid generation of viral variants that possess one or more mutations relative to the original virus strain.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the poor proofreading activity of the viral polymerase.

claim: Many viral mutants are of reduced or unaltered virulence compared to the wild-type parental viral strain.
source: Many viral mutants are of reduced or unaltered virulence compared to the wild-type (WT) parental viral strain (Van den Hoecke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Viral variants that display increased virulence can emerge.
source: However, viral variants that display increased virulence can also emerge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about viral evolution.

claim: There are a higher number of influenza virus variants in individuals that suffer from severe disease.
source: Modelling studies suggest that there are a higher number of influenza virus variants in individuals that suffer from severe disease (Reperant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to modeling studies.

claim: Mutations that are of increased virulence but of reduced fitness are able to replicate in immunocompromised individuals and not in individuals that have a fully competent immune response.
source: This may reflect the fact that mutations that are of increased virulence but of reduced fitness are able to replicate in immunocompromised individuals and not in individuals that have a fully competent immune response.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the observation about viral variants in severe disease.

claim: In individuals with severe disease there may be additional rounds of virus replication, which represent additional opportunities for viral mutagenesis.
source: Alternatively, in individuals with severe disease there may be additional rounds of virus replication, which represent additional opportunities for viral mutagenesis (Reperant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is presented as an alternative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Pregnant mice infected with influenza virus have an increased rate of viral mutations compared to their non-pregnant counterparts.
source: Consistent with these observations, pregnant mice infected with influenza virus have an increased rate of viral mutations compared to their non-pregnant counterparts (Engels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The impaired interferon response of obese mice is thought to drive the emergence of virulent influenza virus variants.
source: Similarly, the impaired interferon response of obese mice is thought to drive the emergence of virulent influenza virus variants (Honce et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Asthma is a host co-morbidity frequently associated with an impaired interferon response.
source: These data raise the question whether asthma, a host co-morbidity frequently associated with an impaired interferon response (Wark et al., 2005; Contoli et al., 2006), also facilitates the emergence of influenza virus variants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic asthma was identified as the single most common underlying medical condition in individuals hospitalised with influenza.
source: During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic asthma was identified as the single most common underlying medical condition in individuals hospitalised with influenza (Nguyen-Van-Tam et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Individuals with asthma have a greater risk of admission to the hospital upon influenza virus infection.
source: Individuals with asthma are known to have a greater risk of (i) admission to the hospital (Neuzil et al., 2000; O'Riordan et al., 2010; Van Kerkhove et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2008), (ii) being treated in the intensive care unit (Bueving et al., 2004; Libster et al., 2010), (iii) requiring a greater number of outpatient visits (Morris et al., 2012; Neuzil et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2008), and (iv) developing pneumonia (O'Riordan et al., 2010; Dawood et al., 2011) upon influenza virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Individuals with asthma have a greater risk of being treated in the intensive care unit upon influenza virus infection.
source: Individuals with asthma are known to have a greater risk of (i) admission to the hospital (Neuzil et al., 2000; O'Riordan et al., 2010; Van Kerkhove et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2008), (ii) being treated in the intensive care unit (Bueving et al., 2004; Libster et al., 2010), (iii) requiring a greater number of outpatient visits (Morris et al., 2012; Neuzil et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2008), and (iv) developing pneumonia (O'Riordan et al., 2010; Dawood et al., 2011) upon influenza virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Individuals with asthma require a greater number of outpatient visits upon influenza virus infection.
source: Individuals with asthma are known to have a greater risk of (i) admission to the hospital (Neuzil et al., 2000; O'Riordan et al., 2010; Van Kerkhove et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2008), (ii) being treated in the intensive care unit (Bueving et al., 2004; Libster et al., 2010), (iii) requiring a greater number of outpatient visits (Morris et al., 2012; Neuzil et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2008), and (iv) developing pneumonia (O'Riordan et al., 2010; Dawood et al., 2011) upon influenza virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Individuals with asthma have a greater risk of developing pneumonia upon influenza virus infection.
source: Individuals with asthma are known to have a greater risk of (i) admission to the hospital (Neuzil et al., 2000; O'Riordan et al., 2010; Van Kerkhove et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2008), (ii) being treated in the intensive care unit (Bueving et al., 2004; Libster et al., 2010), (iii) requiring a greater number of outpatient visits (Morris et al., 2012; Neuzil et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2008), and (iv) developing pneumonia (O'Riordan et al., 2010; Dawood et al., 2011) upon influenza virus infection.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: The majority of patients with asthma were hospitalised for influenza in the absence of an acute asthma attack.
source: Whilst some of these observations may be attributable to the fact that influenza virus can exacerbate the symptoms of asthma (Obuchi et al., 2013), Dawood and colleagues demonstrated that the majority of patients with asthma were hospitalised for influenza in the absence of an acute asthma attack (Dawood et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study by Dawood and colleagues.

claim: Once hospitalised, influenza patients with asthma have a greater survival rate than patients with other conditions.
source: However, a global analysis of pH1N1 cases suggests that once hospitalised, influenza patients with asthma have a greater survival rate than patients with other conditions (Van Kerkhove et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a global analysis.

claim: Mice with the cardinal features of asthma display reduced disease severity following infection with influenza virus.
source: Consistent with these findings, studies using a mouse model of disease actually suggest that mice with the cardinal features of asthma display reduced disease severity following infection with influenza virus (Furuya et al., 2015; Samarasinghe et al., 2014; Ishikawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple mouse studies.

claim: Asthma is a heterogenous disease, consisting of many different phenotypes.
source: However, it is important to recognise that asthma is a heterogenous disease, consisting of many different phenotypes (Svenningsen and Nair, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Different subtypes of asthma may display differing degrees of synergism with influenza virus.
source: It is possible that different subtypes of asthma display differing degrees of synergism with influenza virus.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis to explain contradictory findings in the literature.

claim: Approximately 40% of adults suffer from allergic 'eosinophilic asthma'.
source: Whilst approximately 40% of adults suffer from this allergic 'eosinophilic asthma', a large percentage of asthma patients suffer from non-allergic asthma (i.e. where asthma is observed in the absence of eosinophilic asthma).
evidence: This is stated as epidemiological knowledge about asthma prevalence.

claim: Paucigranulocytic asthma is a subtype where airway remodelling occurs in the absence of eosinophilia or neutrophilia.
source: One such subtype is paucigranulocytic asthma in which airway remodelling occurs in the absence of eosinophilia or neutrophilia.
evidence: This is a definition of the paucigranulocytic asthma phenotype.

claim: In some populations paucigranulocytic asthma can affect up to 40% of asthmatic patients.
source: We chose to focus on paucigranulocytic asthma for this study as (i) the relationship between this specific phenotype of non-allergic asthma and severe influenza has yet to be studied, (ii) in some populations paucigranulocytic asthma can affect up to 40% of asthmatic patients (Schleich et al., 2013), and (iii) paucigranulocytic asthma is associated with an impaired interferon response (Arikkatt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study.

claim: Paucigranulocytic asthma is associated with an impaired interferon response.
source: We chose to focus on paucigranulocytic asthma for this study as (i) the relationship between this specific phenotype of non-allergic asthma and severe influenza has yet to be studied, (ii) in some populations paucigranulocytic asthma can affect up to 40% of asthmatic patients (Schleich et al., 2013), and (iii) paucigranulocytic asthma is associated with an impaired interferon response (Arikkatt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: An early-life PVM infection followed by reinfection with PVM later in life in RAGE-deficient mice promotes airway remodelling characteristic of asthma.
source: In this model, an early-life PVM infection followed by reinfection with PVM later in life in mice deficient in the receptor for advanced glycation endproducts (RAGE), encoded by the Ager gene, promotes airway remodelling characteristic of asthma (Arikkatt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the mouse model used, supported by a citation.

claim: An early and later life PVM infection in RAGE-deficient mice resulted in a significant increase in the number of mucus secreting cells.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017), an early and later life PVM infection in RAGE-deficient mice resulted in a significant increase in the number of mucus secreting cells and ASM mass (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An early and later life PVM infection in RAGE-deficient mice resulted in a significant increase in ASM mass.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017), an early and later life PVM infection in RAGE-deficient mice resulted in a significant increase in the number of mucus secreting cells and ASM mass (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of CXCL1 compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of TNF-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of CCL2 compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IL12 compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IL1b compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IL10 compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Arikkatt et al., 2017) asthmatic mice had significantly lower pulmonary levels of IFN-γ, CXCL1, TNF-α, CCL2, IL12, IL1b, IL10, and IFN-α compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Asthmatic mice infected with IAV lost significantly more body weight over time compared to non-asthmatic control mice.
source: Asthmatic mice infected with IAV lost significantly more body weight over time compared to non-asthmatic control mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Increased weight loss in asthmatic mice was associated with increased IAV replication in the lungs at 6 days post-infection.
source: This was associated with increased IAV replication in the lungs of asthmatic mice at 6 days post-infection (d.p.i)(Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Asthmatic mice showed a significantly impaired type I interferon response following IAV infection, with a downregulation of IFN-α.
source: Furthermore, asthmatic mice showed a significantly impaired type I interferon response, with a downregulation of both IFN-α and interferon inducible MX1 following IAV infection (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Asthmatic mice showed a significantly impaired type I interferon response following IAV infection, with a downregulation of interferon inducible MX1.
source: Furthermore, asthmatic mice showed a significantly impaired type I interferon response, with a downregulation of both IFN-α and interferon inducible MX1 following IAV infection (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Asthmatic host-derived samples showed significantly more within-host viral diversity of the PB1 segment at 6 d.p.i.
source: Asthmatic host-derived samples showed significantly more within-host viral diversity of the PB1 segment at 6 d.p.i. (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was an increase in unique mutations detected in asthmatic compared to non-asthmatic host samples, with 32 and 5, respectively.
source: Overall, there was an increase in unique mutations detected in asthmatic compared to non-asthmatic host samples, with 32 and 5, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data presented in Table 1.

claim: The bulk of the mutations were focused around the priming loop, thumb, and C-terminal extension of PB1.
source: Interestingly, the bulk of the mutations were focused around the priming loop, thumb, and C-terminal extension of PB1.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of mutation locations.

claim: Two unique mouse single nucleotide variants that were unique to asthmatic mouse samples were also detected in clinical samples at a higher frequency in asthmatic patient samples.
source: Strikingly, of the unique mouse single nucleotide variants, two that were unique to asthmatic mouse samples were also detected in clinical samples at a higher frequency in asthmatic patient samples (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of mouse and clinical sequence data in Table 1.

claim: The K691R mutation reached a high enough frequency in two asthmatic mouse samples to alter the consensus sequence.
source: Interestingly, of the mutations identified in the clinical consensus sequence samples, the K691R mutation reached a high enough frequency in two asthmatic mouse samples to alter the consensus sequence.
evidence: This is an observation from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: Viruses in asthmatic lung homogenates replicated to significantly higher titres than those from non-asthmatic lung homogenates at 24 hr post-infection in MDCK cells.
source: The viruses in the asthmatic lung homogenates replicated to significantly higher titres than those from non-asthmatic lung homogenates at 24 hr post-infection in MDCK cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro replication data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The increased replication of viral isolates from asthmatic mice was not associated with a large number of additional in vitro adaptations.
source: Together, these data suggest that the increased replication of viral isolates from asthmatic mice was not associated with a large number of additional in vitro adaptations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing parent and daughter viral populations after in vitro replication.

claim: The C693Y mutation identified exclusively in asthmatic hosts could alter the interaction between PB1 and PB2 within the polymerase heterotrimer.
source: Together, these data suggest that the C693Y mutation identified exclusively in asthmatic hosts could alter the interaction between PB1 and PB2 within the polymerase heterotrimer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural modeling analysis.

claim: The structural modelling of C693Y identified a side chain–side chain interaction in the mutant between PB1 C693Y and PB2 K32 in the third α-helix.
source: The structural modelling of C693Y identified a side chain–side chain interaction in the mutant between PB1 C693Y and PB2 K32 in the third α-helix (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both the PB1 C693Y and P651Q mutations within the PB1 gene increased polymerase activity when compared to the WT virus polymerase.
source: Both the PB1 C693Y and P651Q mutations within the PB1 gene increased polymerase activity when compared to the WT virus polymerase (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by minigenome assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had significantly more weight loss compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
source: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had significantly more weight loss (Figure 8A), lower blood oxygen saturation (Figure 8B), and higher viral titres (Figure 8C) compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had lower blood oxygen saturation compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
source: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had significantly more weight loss (Figure 8A), lower blood oxygen saturation (Figure 8B), and higher viral titres (Figure 8C) compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had higher viral titres compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
source: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had significantly more weight loss (Figure 8A), lower blood oxygen saturation (Figure 8B), and higher viral titres (Figure 8C) compared to mice infected with non-asthmatic host-derived IAV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had a significant upregulation in various anti-viral and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Mice infected with asthmatic host-derived IAV had a significant upregulation in various anti-viral and pro-inflammatory cytokines (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Upon infection of a non-asthmatic host with non-asthmatic-derived IAV, there is an observable divergence in the PB1 haplotype differences as the virus continues to adapt to its host.
source: Furthermore, upon infection of a non-asthmatic host with non-asthmatic-derived IAV, there is an observable divergence in the PB1 haplotype differences as the virus continues to adapt to its host (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by MDS analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Upon infection of a non-asthmatic host with asthmatic-derived IAV, there is a consolidation of the PB1 mutations that arose during the initial infection.
source: By contrast, upon infection of a non-asthmatic host with asthmatic-derived IAV, there is a consolidation of the PB1 mutations that arose during the initial infection (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by MDS analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Asthmatic hosts could facilitate the emergence of new strains that have increased pathogenicity.
source: Together these data suggests that asthmatic hosts could facilitate the emergence of new strains that have increased pathogenicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about viral transmission and pathogenicity.

claim: Mouse studies modelling allergic asthma have suggested that asthma may mediate partial protection from severe influenza.
source: Mouse studies modelling allergic asthma have suggested that asthma may mediate partial protection from severe influenza (Furuya et al., 2015; Samarasinghe et al., 2014; Ishikawa et al., 2012; Doorley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple mouse studies.

claim: Using a mouse model of non-allergic paucigranulocytic asthma, the impaired interferon response is associated with increased influenza severity.
source: Here, using our previously established mouse model of non-allergic paucigranulocytic asthma (Arikkatt et al., 2017), we show that the impaired interferon response (characteristic of this subtype) is associated with increased influenza severity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: An impaired interferon response correlates with an increase in the emergence of influenza viral variants.
source: Recent data suggest that an impaired interferon response correlates with an increase in the emergence of influenza viral variants (Engels et al., 2017; Honce et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: An allogenic pregnant host environment fails to activate the innate immune response, including that of type I interferons during IAV infection.
source: Engels and colleagues demonstrated that an allogenic pregnant host environment fails to activate the innate immune response, including that of type I interferons during IAV infection (Engels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The failure to mount a robust immune response in pregnant hosts was associated with an increased viral load and a higher emergence of viral variants.
source: The failure to mount a robust immune response was associated with an increased viral load and a higher emergence of viral variants (Engels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The decreased type I interferon response within an obese micro-environment corresponded to increased viral replication and enhanced virulence compared to WT mice.
source: More recently, Honce and colleagues demonstrated that the decreased type I interferon response within an obese micro-environment corresponded to increased viral replication and enhanced virulence compared to WT mice (Honce et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The absence of an early immune response in the asthmatic mice may allow for the emergence of viral variants that would otherwise be suppressed in a healthy host.
source: The absence of an early immune response in the asthmatic mice, that is, lack of type I interferon expression, may allow for the emergence of viral variants that would otherwise be suppressed in a healthy host.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: Non-asthmatic host-derived viruses showed host adaption and little sign of morbidity in WT mice.
source: Further to this, non-asthmatic host-derived viruses showed host adaption and little sign of morbidity in WT mice, while asthmatic host-derived virus resulted in increased morbidity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the transmission experiments.

claim: Asthmatic host-derived virus resulted in increased morbidity in WT mice.
source: Further to this, non-asthmatic host-derived viruses showed host adaption and little sign of morbidity in WT mice, while asthmatic host-derived virus resulted in increased morbidity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the transmission experiments.

claim: Viral variants born from an asthmatic host could lead to the emergence of more pathogenic viral strains.
source: This suggests that viral variants born from an asthmatic host could (transmission permitting) lead to the emergence of more pathogenic viral strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The influenza A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase forms dimers of heterotrimers consisting of PA, PB1, and PB2.
source: The influenza A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) forms dimers of heterotrimers consisting of PA, PB1, and PB2 (Fan et al., 2019), with areas of inter-subunit contact stabilising the trimers (Pflug et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Areas of inter-subunit contact stabilise the influenza polymerase trimers.
source: The influenza A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) forms dimers of heterotrimers consisting of PA, PB1, and PB2 (Fan et al., 2019), with areas of inter-subunit contact stabilising the trimers (Pflug et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The β-hairpin within the PB1 thumb domain is responsible for viral replication initiation.
source: The β-hairpin within the PB1 thumb domain is responsible for viral replication initiation, and deletions in this region impair viral replication and growth (Oymans and te Velthuis, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Deletions in the β-hairpin region impair viral replication and growth.
source: The β-hairpin within the PB1 thumb domain is responsible for viral replication initiation, and deletions in this region impair viral replication and growth (Oymans and te Velthuis, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: The P651 residue has previously been shown to be the primary amino acid involved in coordinating terminal initiation during replication.
source: Interestingly, the P651 residue has previously been shown to be the primary amino acid involved in coordinating terminal initiation during replication (Te Velthuis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Glutamine residues have been documented to interact with nucleotide bases.
source: Glutamine residues have been documented to interact with nucleotide bases (Luscombe et al., 2001), and given the position of PB1 P651Q, it is possible that it alters the interaction with the 3ʹ sugar-base of the vRNA or is beneficial to structural conformation during the initiation process.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: PB1 P651Q may alter the interaction with the 3ʹ sugar-base of the vRNA or is beneficial to structural conformation during the initiation process.
source: Glutamine residues have been documented to interact with nucleotide bases (Luscombe et al., 2001), and given the position of PB1 P651Q, it is possible that it alters the interaction with the 3ʹ sugar-base of the vRNA or is beneficial to structural conformation during the initiation process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural knowledge.

claim: The C-terminus of PB1 constitutes the major binding region with the N-terminus of PB2 and has an overall major stabilising effect on the heterotrimer.
source: C693Y and K691R (both of which were identified in asthmatic mice) reside in the first α-helix of the C-terminus, which constitutes the major binding region with the N-terminus of PB2 and has an overall major stabilising effect on the heterotrimer (Pflug et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2009; Te Velthuis and Fodor, 2016; Sugiyama et al., 2009; Poole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of any of the three α-helices within the C-terminus abolishes viral gene expression.
source: Deletion of any of the three α-helices within the C-terminus abolishes viral gene expression (Poole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Double and single mutations in the C-terminus of PB1 alter viral RNA yield.
source: Double and single mutations in the C-terminus of PB1 alter viral RNA yield (Sugiyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The PB1 C693Y and P651Q mutations detected in asthmatic mice resulted in increased viral replication in various epithelial cell lines.
source: Thus cumulatively, the data presented here suggest that the PB1 C693Y and P651Q mutations detected in asthmatic mice resulted in increased viral replication in various epithelial cell lines, and increased polymerase activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by experimental data.
